steps.say: Hypersensitivity has four mechanisms and each one indicates a different disease family. Type 1 is immediate and driven by IgE antibodies. Type 2 is cytotoxic antibody injury of cells. Type 3 is immune complex deposition in vessel walls. Type 4 is late injury by sensitised T cells. This figure illustrates all four mechanisms with clinical examples.
steps.tx: The Gell and Coombs classification divides hypersensitivity into four mechanisms. Type I is IgE mediated immediate mast cell degranulation (rapid allergy and anaphylaxis). Type II is antibody mediated cytotoxic injury (warm autoimmune haemolysis and Goodpasture disease). Type III is **immune complex** deposition (clumps of antigen plus antibody in SLE and serum sickness). Type IV is delayed T cell hypersensitivity (contact dermatitis and the tuberculin test). Name the mechanism first, because each one indicates different testing and therapy.

vis.alt: Diagram of Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity types 1 to 4 with mechanisms and clinical examples.
vis.caption: Four mechanisms cover allergy, cytotoxic injury, complex deposition, and delayed T cell reactions. Each mechanism indicates its own workup. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Anaphylaxis requires intramuscular adrenaline in the mid thigh without any delay. The adult dose is drawn from 1 to 1000 strength ampoules. Children require weight based dosing by the same intramuscular route. Every dose is repeated at short intervals until the circulation has fully recovered. Intravenous boluses are never given outside a monitored bed.
steps.tx: Anaphylaxis (sudden multisystem allergic collapse) is reversed with prompt intramuscular **adrenaline** (epinephrine, the resuscitation drug that constricts vessels and opens airways) given into the anterolateral mid thigh. The adult amount is **0.3 mg to 0.5 mg** while children get **0.01 mg per kg**, drawn from **1:1,000** ampoules (**1 mg per mL**) and repeated every **5 to 15 minutes**. Intravenous boluses stay inside monitored beds, because a thigh injection is the safest effective opening move.

steps.say: Tryptase confirms anaphylaxis after the event has settled. It peaks in the first couple of hours and is gone by the next day. A qualifying rise is defined against the baseline pair. The peak and baseline samples are drawn whenever the diagnosis is uncertain.
steps.tx: Serum total **tryptase** (a mast cell granule enzyme) rises transiently after systemic degranulation, peaking **1 to 2 hours** after onset and returning to baseline within **24 hours**. A meaningful acute rise is confirmed when peak tryptase exceeds **1.2 times** baseline plus **2 ng per mL**. Draw one sample at 1 to 2 hours and one baseline sample later, because a single value without baseline cannot confirm the event.

vis.alt: Mast cell degranulation effects with adrenaline receptor treatment sites in anaphylaxis.
vis.caption: Degranulation releases tryptase and histamine while adrenaline acts at alpha and beta receptors. Paired tryptase samples confirm the event. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Chronic spontaneous urticaria is defined by 6 weeks of wheals without a trigger. Quadrupled antihistamines come first. Omalizumab 300 mg every 4 weeks is the answer when they fail. Most other wheals with a trigger require trigger control instead.
steps.tx: Chronic spontaneous **urticaria** (recurrent itchy wheals) is defined by pruritic wheals, angioedema, or both lasting **6 weeks** or longer without an identifiable trigger. Second generation H1 antihistamines at up to quadrupled doses come first. Refractory disease responds dramatically to **omalizumab** (monoclonal anti IgE antibody) at **300 mg** subcutaneously every **4 weeks**. Wheals with a physical trigger instead require trigger avoidance, because omalizumab is reserved for spontaneous disease.

steps.say: Hereditary angioedema is a bradykinin disease, not a histamine disease. SERPING1 mutations remove the C1 inhibitor brake. Swelling arrives without itch or wheals, with colic and throat closure. This figure traces the pathway from missing inhibitor to swelling.
steps.tx: Hereditary angioedema (**HAE**, episodic subcutaneous swelling disease) is an autosomal dominant disorder from **SERPING1** mutations causing C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency (type 1, **85 percent**) or dysfunction (type 2, **15 percent**). Missing inhibition produces excess **bradykinin** (a permeability peptide), giving non pruritic non pitting swelling without urticaria, recurrent abdominal attacks, and laryngeal edema. Swelling without wheals indicates bradykinin, while swelling with wheals indicates histamine.

vis.alt: Pathway of C1 inhibitor deficiency causing bradykinin mediated angioedema with management options.
vis.caption: Missing C1 inhibitor releases bradykinin and swelling without wheals. The pathway indicates why antihistamines fail. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: A low C4 is the screening clue in hereditary angioedema with above 95 percent sensitivity. Type 1 is the form with low protein while type 2 is the form with normal protein and poor function. C1q is normal in hereditary disease and low in acquired disease. All three levels are ordered together.
steps.tx: Laboratory screening for HAE reveals persistently depressed serum **C4** (above **95 percent** sensitivity) in quiet and active phases alike. Type 1 shows decreased C1 inhibitor protein, while type 2 shows normal or elevated protein with impaired functional activity. **C1q** levels are characteristically normal in HAE but depressed in acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency (lymphoma associated disease). A low C4 with normal C1q indicates hereditary disease, while a low C1q points to acquired disease.

Low C4, normal protein, low function

steps.say: Bradykinin attacks are unmoved by adrenaline, antihistamines, and steroids. Specific therapy is C1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant, or ecallantide. ACE inhibitor swelling follows the same bradykinin rule. Lifelong ACE avoidance is required after even a single episode.
steps.tx: Acute HAE attacks do not improve with adrenaline, antihistamines, or glucocorticoids, because none of them blocks bradykinin. Attacks require plasma derived or recombinant **C1 inhibitor** concentrate, **icatibant** (a blocker of the bradykinin B2 receptor), or **ecallantide** (an inhibitor of plasma kallikrein). Angioedema from angiotensin converting enzyme (**ACE**) inhibitors runs on the same bradykinin pathway, explains up to **30 percent** of emergency angioedema visits, hits tongue and pharynx months after the first tablet, and forces lifelong ACE avoidance with careful ARB use.

points: HAE and ACE swelling are bradykinin driven
